slides.text:
A rune is a number, so you can ask what kind of character it is: a letter, a digit, a space, punctuation, a capital.

The `unicode` package answers those questions for every alphabet. Session 1 sorts characters, session 2 handles punctuation, symbols and numbers, and session 3 checks whole texts and scripts. Changing the case of a whole string is in `strings-package`.
Each function takes one rune and answers true or false. They know every alphabet, not only English. Pseudo code, not Go:
slides.code:
isLetter('ñ') -> true
isDigit('ñ')  -> false
isSpace(' ')  -> true
toUpper('é')  -> 'É'

exercises.title: Ask what a character is
exercises.guide: The `unicode` package answers questions about a rune.

chunks.guide: `IsLetter` is true for a letter of any alphabet, not only English ones.

notes.text: Takes a rune and answers true or false.

chunks.guide: `IsDigit` is true for characters that are digits.
`IsSpace` is true for a space, a tab or a line break.

output.text:
true
true
true
false
true
false

exercises.title: Count each kind
exercises.guide: Count each kind of character in a text.

chunks.guide: One counter for each kind of character.
Test every character, and add to the matching counter.
The dot is none of the three, so nobody counts it.

exercises.title: Case of a rune
exercises.guide: Check the case of a rune, and convert it.

chunks.guide: `IsUpper` and `IsLower` check the case of a letter.
A digit has no case, so both answers are false.
`ToUpper` and `ToLower` return the converted rune. `string` turns it into text.

notes.text: Gives back a rune, so wrap it in string to print the letter.

output.text:
true false
false false
É
ñ

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.explanation: `Ñ` is a letter and a capital, so it is not lower case.

exercises.title: Flip the case
exercises.guide: Convert the letter to a capital, then check that the result is one.

slides.text: Punctuation and symbols are two different groups, and a number is a wider idea than a digit. Pseudo code:
slides.code:
punctuation: ! , . ? - _
symbol:      $ + = < >
digit:       0 1 2 ... 9
number:      digits, and also ½ ²

slides.text: These functions are ideal rules for `strings.Map` and `strings.FieldsFunc`: they decide what to keep or where to split.

exercises.title: Punctuation and symbols
exercises.guide: Unicode splits marks into punctuation and symbols.

chunks.guide: `IsPunct` is true for marks like the exclamation point and the comma.
`IsSymbol` covers signs like the dollar and the plus.
The groups do not overlap: a dollar is a symbol, not punctuation.

notes.text: Unicode files the dollar sign as a symbol.

output.text:
true true
true true
false false

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.explanation: A hyphen is punctuation, but `+` and `=` are symbols.

exercises.title: Digits and numbers
exercises.guide: Some numeric characters are not digits.

chunks.guide: Digits of other alphabets are digits too. This one is the Arabic three.
A fraction is a number but not a digit. `IsNumber` accepts both.

notes.text: Wider than a digit: fractions and superscripts count.

exercises.title: Strip the punctuation
exercises.guide: Remove the punctuation from a text.

chunks.guide: Return `-1` to drop a rune, and the rune itself to keep it.
`Map` applies the function to every rune of the text.
Hyphens, parentheses and dots all count as punctuation.

exercises.title: Split into words
exercises.guide: Split a text into its words, whatever separates them.

chunks.guide: Anything that is not a letter works as a separator.
Several separators in a row count as one.
chunks.text:
text := "go, rust; and zig!"
    words := strings.FieldsFunc(text, notLetter)
    fmt.Println(words, len(words))

exercises.title: Marks of any kind
exercises.guide: Make `isMark` true for punctuation, or for a symbol.

slides.text: To check a whole text, test every rune and stop at the first failure. Pseudo code:

A `unicode` function can also be handed straight to a `strings` helper, as the rule it applies.

Watch what you pass in: a rune, not a byte.

exercises.title: Is it only letters?
exercises.guide: Write a function that says whether a text has only letters.

chunks.guide: Stop at the first character that is not a letter.
If nothing failed, the text is a word, unless it is empty.
Accents count as letters, digits do not.

exercises.title: Capitalize a word
exercises.guide: Write a function that capitalizes the first letter of a word.

chunks.guide: Work on runes, so a first letter with an accent is safe.
An empty word has no first letter to convert.
Convert only the first rune and keep the rest.
The accent is kept when the letter changes case.

exercises.title: Lower the first letter
exercises.guide: Make the first letter of the word lower case.

exercises.title: Check the script
exercises.guide: Find out which writing system a character belongs to.

chunks.guide: `unicode.Is` checks a rune against a script, like the Han characters of Chinese.

notes.text: Pass the script first, then the rune to test.

chunks.guide: Other scripts have their own tables, like Latin and Cyrillic.
Count the characters of one script in a mixed text.

exercises.title: Pass the function
exercises.guide: Hand the unicode functions to the strings helpers.

chunks.guide: `IndexFunc` finds the first rune a function accepts. Give it a `unicode` function as it is.

notes.text: No parentheses: the function itself is handed over.

chunks.text:
text := "room 42, floor 7"
    first := strings.IndexFunc(
        text, unicode.IsDigit)
    fmt.Println(first)

chunks.guide: `ContainsFunc` asks whether any rune fits.
`TrimFunc` cuts both ends while the function says true.

exercises.title: Bytes are not runes
exercises.guide: Count punctuation by bytes and by runes, and compare.

chunks.guide: Walk the text by index. Each `text[i]` is a byte.

notes.text: Turns a single byte into a rune, right or wrong.

chunks.guide: Now walk the runes with `range`.
The counts differ: one byte of `á` looks like `¡` when taken alone.
